samples.text:
The line graph shows the average price of a new home in one country from 2000 to 2024, and the bar chart shows the house prices compared to average earnings in the same years.

Overall, house prices went up in most years and houses became less affordable because the ratio also increased.

In 2000 a new home cost $96 thousand on average. The price increased quickly to $148 thousand in 2004 and $186 thousand in 2008. However, in 2012 there was a small fall to $172 thousand. After that the price rose again in every period and it reached $215 thousand in 2016, $251 thousand in 2020 and $298 thousand in 2024. It means the price was more than three times higher than in 2000.

The bar chart has a similar pattern. In 2000 the house price was 4.1 times the average annual earnings, and it went up to 5.6 in 2004 and 6.3 in 2008. Then it dropped to 5.7 in 2012, but after that it increase to 6.6, 7.2 and finally 8.1 in 2024. This is almost double of the 2000 ratio.
samples.why: Overview present but loosely expressed · both visuals covered accurately with every figure listed · adequate but mechanical linking · limited vocabulary · errors in verb form, comparatives and word choice.

samples.text:
The line graph illustrates how the average price of a new home in one country changed between 2000 and 2024, while the bar chart compares average house prices with average yearly earnings over the same period.

Overall, new home prices rose substantially, apart from a slight dip in 2012, and houses became increasingly expensive relative to earnings, following a very similar pattern.

In 2000, a new home cost US$96 thousand on average. Prices climbed rapidly to US$186 thousand in 2008, nearly double the initial figure, before falling back slightly to US$172 thousand in 2012. From then on, they increased steadily, reaching US$215 thousand in 2016 and US$251 thousand in 2020, and peaking at US$298 thousand in 2024, more than three times the 2000 level.

The ratio of house prices to earnings shows the same trend. At the start of the period, an average house cost 4.1 times the average annual salary, and this figure rose to 6.3 in 2008. It then fell to 5.7 in 2012, but it has risen continuously since then, reaching 7.2 in 2020 and 8.1 in 2024. This means that, compared to earnings, housing was almost twice as expensive in 2024 than in 2000.
samples.why: Clear overview linking the two measures · key features highlighted with accurate comparisons · good progression and cohesion · some less common vocabulary (relative to, dip) · two minor grammatical slips.

samples.text:
The line graph tracks the average price of a new home in one country from 2000 to 2024, and the bar chart expresses average house prices as a multiple of average annual earnings over the same years.

Both measures rose markedly across the period, interrupted only by a modest dip in 2012, indicating that housing became considerably less affordable.

The average new home cost US$96 thousand in 2000, but prices increased sharply over the next eight years to US$186 thousand. After easing to US$172 thousand in 2012, they resumed their upward path, climbing to US$251 thousand by 2020 and US$298 thousand by 2024, more than three times their 2000 level.

The price-to-earnings ratio mirrored this pattern closely. In 2000, a home cost 4.1 times the average annual wage, a figure that had climbed to 6.3 by 2008 before slipping to 5.7 in 2012. Thereafter, the ratio rose without interruption, to 6.6 in 2016, 7.2 in 2020 and 8.1 in 2024. In other words, relative to earnings, housing was almost twice as expensive at the end of the period as it had been at the start, although this near doubling was far smaller than the more than threefold rise in prices themselves.
samples.why: Concise overview drawing a valid conclusion from both visuals · figures selected and compared precisely · sophisticated cohesion (In other words, Thereafter) · precise vocabulary · wide range of structures, error-free.
